---
title: "Exercise 4 · Write Your First Skill"
subtitle: "Package a task you actually repeat — the course's core deliverable"
---

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Time:** ~12 min · **Pairs with:** [Skills & Workflows](../skills.qmd) · **Goal:** a working, reusable skill that captures *how you like a recurring task done*. This is the thing you take home.
:::

## 1 · Pick a task you repeat (2 min)

Choose one recurring task where you keep re-explaining your preferences. Steal one of these if nothing jumps out:

- **Table 1 builder** — baseline characteristics to your house style.
- **Figure formatter** — apply your (or a journal's) figure specs to a plot.
- **Project scaffold** — set up a reproducible repo the way you always do.
- **Reviewer-response drafter** — comments + notes → point-by-point response.
- **Model diagnostics** — run your standard checks on a fitted model.

## 2 · Draft it from the template (5 min)

Open the [`SKILL.md` template](../templates/SKILL.md). Fill in the four parts:

```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-name>
description: >
  <ONE specific sentence: what it does and WHEN to use it. This is how
  the agent decides to invoke it — be concrete.>
---

# <Skill title>

## When to use
<The situation that should trigger this skill.>

## How to do it
1. <step>
2. <step>  (name the packages / functions you prefer)
3. <where the output goes and what it looks like>

## Conventions & guardrails
- <your style choices>
- Show me the result before saving. Never fabricate values.
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Let the agent help you write it
You can bootstrap the skill by describing the task once and asking:
```text
Turn this into a skill file: I regularly build a Table 1 of baseline
characteristics by treatment arm using gtsummary, median [IQR] for
continuous and n (%) for categorical, saved as a gt table. Write it in
the SKILL.md format with a specific description and guardrails.
```
Then refine the `description` and guardrails yourself.
:::

## 3 · Install it where Claude Code will find it (2 min)

Save the file into your skills folder (project-level so it travels with the repo):

```bash
mkdir -p .claude/skills/table-one
# save your file as .claude/skills/table-one/SKILL.md
```

(Adjust the name to your skill.) Commit it:

```bash
git add .claude/skills
git commit -m "Add table-one skill"
```

## 4 · Test it on real input (3 min)

Start a fresh session and trigger the skill with a natural request — **don't** name the skill explicitly; see if the `description` makes it fire:

```text
I have a cleaned data frame with age, sex, and treatment arm. Build me a
baseline characteristics table.
```

Watch whether the agent applies *your* conventions from the skill. If it doesn't fire, your `description` probably isn't specific enough about *when* to use it — tighten it and retry.

## You're done when…

- [ ] You have a `SKILL.md` with a specific `description` and clear steps.
- [ ] It includes at least one **guardrail** ("show me before saving" / "never fabricate").
- [ ] It's saved in your skills folder and committed.
- [ ] A natural-language request **triggered** the skill and produced output in your style.

::: {.callout-note}
## Share it
A skill is just a file in git. `git push`, send a labmate the repo, and they `git pull` — now your lab shares an executable convention. This is how a workflow spreads.
:::
